title: Near-linear equivalence testing for propositional Horn theories
formal: Can equivalence of two propositional Horn CNF formulas F and G be decided deterministically in \(O(N\log(N+2))\) time, where N is the total number of literal occurrences plus clause delimiters in their explicit input?
definitions:
A clause is a disjunction of literals containing at most one positive literal. A Horn CNF is a conjunction of such clauses. Negative-only clauses, unit clauses, an empty clause and an empty conjunction are allowed. Equivalence means that F and G have the same truth value on every Boolean assignment to the union of their variable sets, not merely that they are both satisfiable or have the same least model.

Input variables are integer identifiers in {1,…,v}, with v≤N+1; unused identifiers need not be listed. The input is an explicit array of clauses and signed identifiers, with each identifier and delimiter in O(1) words. Use a word-RAM with Theta(log(N+2))-bit words and unit-cost arithmetic, comparisons, bit operations and memory access. The bound includes input processing and any indexing; there is no entailment oracle. Redundant clauses and repeated literals may occur and count toward N. The cost definition includes delimiters so inputs with many empty clauses are not declared to have zero length. A linear-time algorithm would satisfy this target, but the stated near-linear bound is the selected question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked deterministic algorithm and its worst-case total time bound, or prove the bound impossible in this machine model. Linear-time Horn satisfiability alone is insufficient because equivalence quantifies over all assignments. Conditional fine-grained lower bounds must state their assumptions.
context: Kleine Büning’s slides distinguish Horn satisfiability, implication and equivalence questions. The card asks for a near-linear equivalence test, not merely a single satisfiability test.
why: A near-linear equivalence algorithm would make comparison of entire Horn consequence theories nearly as cheap as reading them.
